themes: Validation of fully automated plasma p-tau217 immunoassay
Comparison of primary and secondary care diagnostic accuracy
Impact of age and comorbidities on Alzheimer's biomarkers
one_line: A fully automated plasma p-tau217 immunoassay accurately detects Alzheimer's disease pathology in primary and secondary care, though older patients may require a two-cutoff approach to maintain optimal performance.
summary: The study evaluated a fully automated plasma p-tau217 immunoassay (Lumipulse) for detecting Alzheimer's disease pathology across four secondary care cohorts and one primary care cohort, comprising 1,767 total participants. Using predefined cutoffs, the assay achieved high accuracy (89–91% in secondary care, 85% in primary care). While accuracy remained high across most demographics and comorbidities—including chronic kidney disease—it was significantly lower in older individuals (aged 80 and above). Implementing a two-cutoff approach improved overall accuracy to 92–94% but left 12–17% of participants in an intermediate zone requiring further diagnostic testing. The automated assay performed comparably to high-performing mass spectrometry-based methods in secondary care, although the mass spectrometry %p-tau217 ratio proved more robust against age-related performance drops in primary care.

key_claims.claim: Plasma p-tau217 measured by a fully automated Lumipulse immunoassay accurately identifies AD pathology.
key_claims.evidence: Areas under the receiver operating characteristic curves of 0.93–0.96; accuracies of 89–91% in secondary care and 85% in primary care using a single cutoff.

key_claims.claim: A two-cutoff approach improves diagnostic accuracy but yields an intermediate classification zone.
key_claims.evidence: Using two cutoffs increased accuracies to 92–94% in secondary and primary care, while excluding 12–17% of participants who fell into the intermediate zone.

key_claims.claim: Assay accuracy is negatively affected by older age but not by chronic kidney disease or cognitive stage.
key_claims.evidence: Accuracy was significantly lower in participants aged 73–80 (87%) and ≥80 years (83%) compared with those <73 years (91%); accuracy remained stable across CKD, sex, and APOE statuses.
key_claims.location: Results (Effects of demographic factors and comorbidities) / Fig. 2

key_claims.claim: The plasma p-tau217:Aβ42 ratio does not improve overall accuracy compared to p-tau217 alone but reduces the number of intermediate results.
key_claims.evidence: Accuracy was similar to p-tau217 alone, but intermediate results were reduced from 15–16% to 7–10% when using the two-cutoff approach.
key_claims.location: Results (Comparison of plasma p-tau217 and the p-tau217:Aβ42 ratio)

methods.design: Retrospective analysis of independent prospective cohorts
methods.population: Participants with cognitive symptoms (subjective cognitive decline, mild cognitive impairment, or dementia) in primary and secondary care clinics

funding_and_conflicts: Funded by Swedish Research Council, Alzheimer's Association, GHR Foundation, ERC, Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation, and others. Multiple authors report extensive competing interests including consultancy, speaker fees, and research support from diagnostics and pharmaceutical companies (e.g., Roche, Biogen, Eisai, Eli Lilly); C2N coauthors are salaried employees or consultants for C2N Diagnostics.
limitations: Limited to European cohorts, requiring validation in more diverse global populations.
Slightly lower performance of the Lumipulse assay compared to mass spectrometry-based %p-tau217 in primary care settings and older populations.
red_flags: Extensive financial ties of multiple authors to diagnostic companies and Alzheimer's drug manufacturers, including C2N Diagnostics and Roche.

A subgroup of primary care participants (n=87) had their outcome defined by amyloid PET instead of the primary CSF reference standard, although the authors conducted a sensitivity analysis excluding them.
